newsitem.title: CANADA: High winds threaten Canada flood barriers.
newsitem.headline: High winds threaten Canada flood barriers.

text.p: Brisk winds were forecast for flood-ravaged southern Manitoba on Monday, raising new fears that high waves on the huge lake that now covers the region could threaten dikes protecting mostly evacuated towns.

The Red River, which continued to swallow up vast tracts of rural land in the western Canadian province, was estimated to be 18 miles (29 km) wide at the border with the United States. Hundreds of people had yet to be rescued.

"The effect of the wind is twofold: one is it's going to give the sandbag dikes quite a pounding. On top of that, if some of those dikes begin to give way because of the wind and the waves, it will become increasingly difficult to mount any type of rescue operation," Emergency Measures Organisation spokeswoman Debbie MacKenzie said.

About 17,000 people have been evacuated from towns and farms in the swamped Red River valley south of Winnipeg as the "Red Sea" has spread slowly northward. More than 3,000 were given temporary refuge in a Winnipeg sports arena.

But by Sunday an estimated 400 people had yet to leave their homes in rural communities protected by temporary barriers and police and military personnel were only able to evacuate some of them by boat and helicopter before nightfall.

Up to 25 percent of the sandbag walls built in southern Manitba to protect homes from the murky torrent had failed, even before wind gusts whipped up waves, officials said. "It's really bad news -- sad for those people," MacKenzie said.

The crest of the flooding river, which already devastated vast areas of the Dakotas and Minnesota, may have passed through the border town of Emerson, Manitoba, but officals were not sure. Dikes surrounding the now-evacuated town of 750 were built about 5 feet (1.5 metres) above Sunday's highest level.
Larger towns in the region were shored up by wider "ring" dikes and officials and residents were optimistic they would stand up to the floodwaters better than thin sandbag walls.

Just southwest of of Winnipeg, hundreds of soldiers and a phalanx of earthmoving machines continued feverishly to build a 25-mile (40 km) earthen wall to protect the city against the spreading lake. The planned length was increased over the weekend as floodwaters came within sight of the construction.
If the hastily built dike failed, water would reach Winnipeg within six hours and an estimated 10,000 people in the city would be forced to leave their homes.

Throughout Winnipeg, a city of 650,000, flood preparations remained at a fever pitch as sandbag walls continued to be raised by thousands of volunteers in hopes of protecting low-lying neighbourhoods. Residents of 600 homes have been told by city officials they must evacuate.

In Grand Forks, North Dakota, which was devastated by the flood last week, more of the city of 50,000 was reopened to residents returning for what will be a massive cleanup of damage that some estimates put at $1 billion.
